paragraphs: Image super-resolution models learn to restore detail from degraded images, but their performance can depend heavily on how their training images were damaged. When the degradation encountered during use differs from the training assumption, restoration can fail. This paper addresses that mismatch without trying to manually enumerate every possible degradation.

The proposed adversarial neural degradation model, AND, learns alongside a restoration network under a minmax training objective. The two networks have opposing roles: the degradation model produces challenging damaged images, while the restoration model learns to recover them. This joint training can produce a broad range of complex, nonlinear degradation effects without explicit supervision of the degradation process.

The paper reports better generalization to previously unseen degradation variants and substantially improved restoration of real-world images compared with the current state of the art. The contribution is a learned way to broaden the restoration challenges encountered during training. Its stated benefit is improved robustness to degradation mismatch, rather than a requirement to specify all possible real-world damage in advance.
neurips-2023-and-adversarial-neural-degr.tldr: AND jointly trains a degradation network and a restoration network to improve super-resolution on unseen and real-world degradations.

paragraphs: A classifier can learn an attribute that happens to correlate with a label instead of learning a relationship that remains useful after deployment. Methods that suppress these shortcuts often assume someone already knows which attributes are spurious. AutoACER addresses the harder situation where that information is unavailable.

The method estimates attributes’ causal effects on labels, uses those estimates to identify spurious attributes, and penalizes the classifier’s reliance on them. Causal effects cannot always be identified from the available information. The paper describes two data-generating processes where identification is possible, keeping that condition separate from its broader empirical findings.

Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets, AutoACER improves a measure of dependence on spurious attributes while achieving similar or better accuracy. It also empirically reduces reliance when causal estimates are noisy or unidentified. A supporting result in a simplified linear classification setting shows that correctly ranking causal effects across attributes is sufficient to select the correct classifier; precise effect estimates are not required in that setting.
neurips-2023-causal-effect-regularizatio.tldr: AutoACER uses estimated causal effects to identify and suppress spurious attributes, with empirical robustness and a conditional ranking-based guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate multiple times when the probability distribution of a multivariate time series changes. The observations may have short-range dependence, so nearby measurements need not be independent. Rather than specifying a fixed parametric family, the analysis assumes distributions with Hölder-smooth densities that remain constant within successive time segments.

The main contribution describes the limiting distributions of estimated change times. These results cover both changes whose smallest jump shrinks as the sample grows and changes whose smallest jump stays constant. Characterizing how estimates fluctuate around the true change times supports statistical inference beyond simply reporting a detected boundary.

The analysis also yields an estimator for accurately locating changes and a consistent block-based estimator of long-run variance, which accounts for variability in dependent observations. Numerical studies complement the theoretical results. The findings therefore connect detection and inference in a setting that permits multivariate, nonparametric data, while retaining the stated smoothness, dependence, and piecewise-constant distribution assumptions.
neurips-2023-change-point-detection-and-.tldr: The paper develops change-point estimators and limiting distributions for multivariate time series with smooth densities and short-range dependence.

paragraphs: A multiplayer game can have several Nash equilibria, and the equilibrium selected may matter for an additional objective. This paper studies computing an equilibrium that optimizes such an objective. One motivating case involves independently acting team members who want an equilibrium that minimizes an adversary’s utility.

The problem can be expressed as a mixed-integer bilinear program, but representing interactions introduces many products of variables. Those bilinear terms make the optimization difficult. The authors develop a framework based on correlation plans and an algorithm called CRM that uses relationships among those plans to organize the formulation.

CRM improves the optimization in two connected ways: it reduces the feasible region created by convex relaxation, and it limits the number of correlation plans to reduce bilinear terms. The paper reports significant reductions in time complexity and cases where CRM is several orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art baseline. These findings show that the formulation itself can make objective-driven equilibrium computation substantially more tractable.
neurips-2023-computing-optimal-nash-equi.tldr: CRM makes optimal Nash equilibrium computation faster by reducing bilinear terms and tightening the relaxed optimization problem.

paragraphs: Graph property prediction often has few labeled examples for a particular task, despite the availability of many unlabeled graphs. A common strategy learns representations through self-supervised tasks before fine-tuning. The paper argues that what those preliminary tasks teach can be misaligned with, or even conflict with, the eventual prediction goal.

The proposed approach uses unlabeled graphs to create additional task-specific training data. A diffusion model learns from the larger graph collection, and two new objectives guide its denoising process using each task’s labeled examples. The resulting outputs are graphs together with labels intended to help that task’s prediction model.

Experiments report significantly better performance than fifteen existing methods across fifteen tasks. The contribution makes the use of unlabeled information concrete: it appears as generated labeled examples that augment the predictor’s training set. This provides a different route for transferring knowledge from a broad graph collection, with task relevance built into generation rather than left solely to later fine-tuning.
neurips-2023-data-centric-learning-from-.tldr: A diffusion model turns unlabeled graph collections into task-specific labeled examples that improve graph property prediction.

paragraphs: Representing a graph by factorizing its adjacency matrix can struggle with heterophily: connections between nodes that are dissimilar. This paper introduces a factorization that assigns two nonnegative vectors to each node. The representation is designed to account interpretably for both similarity-based connections and links across differences.

The authors prove that the model can exactly represent graphs with low arboricity, a sparsity property satisfied by many real-world networks. This guarantee has broader scope than the closest previous bound based on low maximum degree. The proof also applies to related models, extending the theoretical contribution beyond the proposed factorization.

Symmetry and nonnegativity give the representation another useful property: fitting it inherently discovers node communities. Predicted links can then be explained through those communities, connecting expressiveness with interpretation. Experiments on real-world networks demonstrate effectiveness for community detection and link prediction. The central result is therefore both representational and practical: a condition for exact graph representation accompanies a model whose fitted structure helps explain its predictions.
neurips-2023-exact-representation-of-spa.tldr: A symmetric factorization with two nonnegative vectors per node captures heterophily and exactly represents graphs with low arboricity.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train collaboratively without sharing their private training data, but their datasets can differ substantially. Clients may have different label frequencies, different input features, or both. Fed-CO2 addresses these two forms of heterogeneity within one framework, where earlier work often considered them separately.

Each client uses cooperating online and offline models. The online model learns general knowledge shared across clients, while the locally trained offline model learns knowledge specific to that client. An intra-client transfer mechanism supports mutual learning between the models, and an inter-client mechanism aims to improve generalization across feature domains.

Experiments show that Fed-CO2 outperforms a broad range of personalized federated learning methods when label skew and feature skew occur separately or together. Convergence analyses in a simplified setting support the empirical results. The approach matters because it gives shared and local knowledge explicit roles, then connects them through cooperation to address variation in both what clients observe and which labels they possess.
neurips-2023-fed-co-2-cooperation-of-onl.tldr: Fed-CO2 combines shared and local models to improve federated learning under both label and feature distribution differences.

paragraphs: People can look at a static scene and infer a sequence of events: what may have happened, what someone is trying to do, and what might happen next. This paper develops a computational account of that ability. The challenge is explaining rapid, flexible inference even for situations a person has not encountered before.

The authors propose a Monte Carlo algorithm, which forms inferences through sampling. Its key technical insight connects this reasoning problem to Monte Carlo path tracing, a method from computer graphics. That connection makes techniques developed for tracing paths in graphics applicable to reasoning about events and the people involved in them.

The algorithm’s inferences correlate well with human intuitions across a variety of domains while using a small number of samples described as cognitively plausible. This supports the model as an account of how limited computation could produce rich interpretations of a snapshot. The stated result concerns agreement with human judgments, connecting an efficient sampling method to the flexibility of everyday social and temporal reasoning.
neurips-2023-inferring-the-future-by-ima.tldr: A sampling algorithm inspired by graphics path tracing models human inferences about past and future events from static scenes.

paragraphs: Increasing training-data scale can also change the harmful content that models encounter. This paper examines that issue through a comparative audit of LAION-400M and LAION-2B, two vision-language datasets assembled from internet material. The focus is how hateful content changes with dataset scale and whether existing filtering adequately addresses it.

The authors combine qualitative assessment with a quantitative measure called Hate Content Rate. They report a nearly 12% increase in hate content with scale in the audited datasets. This finding makes dataset composition part of the scaling discussion, alongside the more commonly emphasized benefits of larger models and larger training collections.

The audit also finds that filtering based on image-only Not Safe For Work scores does not remove all harmful accompanying text. Small amounts of hateful, targeted, and aggressive text remain even with conservative filtering. This matters for multimodal curation because an image-based assessment does not fully characterize its paired alt-text. The paper uses these findings to discuss dataset curation and use, rather than treating greater scale as sufficient evidence of better training data.
neurips-2023-into-the-laions-den-investi.tldr: An audit of two LAION datasets finds increased hate content with scale and harmful text that survives image-based filtering.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting occurs when a model fits noisy training observations yet remains statistically consistent. Prior results suggested that typical kernel regression methods and wide neural networks needed growing input dimension for this behavior. This paper identifies estimator smoothness as the decisive issue in its fixed-dimensional analysis.

The authors show that benign overfitting requires sufficiently large derivatives, which allow an estimator to change sharply. They extend inconsistency results to more kernels and to models that do not exactly interpolate, ruling out benign overfitting with moderate derivatives in fixed dimension. Conversely, a sequence of kernels combining smooth behavior with sharp spikes makes benign overfitting possible.

Using neural tangent kernels, the paper transfers these insights to wide neural networks. It proves that infinite-width ReLU networks do not exhibit benign overfitting in the studied setting, but adding small high-frequency fluctuations to the activation can change that outcome. Experiments show that such modified networks can overfit and still generalize well on low-dimensional datasets. The results connect generalization to local sharpness rather than input dimension alone.
neurips-2023-mind-the-spikes-benign-over.tldr: The paper shows how sufficiently sharp estimator variation enables benign overfitting in fixed dimension, including in modified wide neural networks.

paragraphs: Generating realistic graphs requires capturing how nodes and edges depend on one another. The paper identifies oversmoothing as a problem in existing neural graph generators: graph convolution can blur distinctions and make high-frequency node and edge characteristics difficult to preserve. Realism therefore depends on more than representing broad graph structure.

Wave-GD models node and edge signals together in a shared graph wavelet space. Wavelets provide multiple resolutions for describing variation, letting the model capture dependencies at different scales. A score-based diffusion model operates with this representation to generate synthetic graphs whose node and edge frequency characteristics resemble those of real graphs.

Experiments on four representative benchmark datasets report better performance than existing approaches. These results support the value of jointly modeling nodes and edges while preserving information across resolutions. The contribution is specifically aimed at the loss of fine variation through oversmoothing, and the reported findings suggest that spectral structure is useful for improving graph generation fidelity across the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2023-multi-resolution-spectral-c.tldr: Wave-GD combines graph wavelets and diffusion to preserve node–edge dependencies and frequency characteristics across multiple resolutions.

paragraphs: Smoothness describes how much a function can change as its input changes. Traditional Hölder smoothness uses a worst-case measure, even when the most irregular regions have little probability under the data distribution. This paper develops an average Hölder smoothness measure that reflects where data actually occur and can be much smaller.

The authors prove upper and lower prediction-risk bounds for both realizable regression and agnostic regression with noise. The rates improve previous results, including the special case of average Lipschitz smoothness. In the realizable setting, the lower bound matches the upper rate up to logarithmic factors, establishing the minimax rate to that precision.

The average measure depends on an unknown distribution, so the learner lacks an explicit function-class representation needed to directly execute empirical risk minimization. The paper nevertheless provides separate learning algorithms achieving nearly optimal rates. Its results apply to totally bounded metric spaces and use their intrinsic geometry. Together, these findings show how distribution-sensitive smoothness can yield substantially sharper guarantees than a worst-case description.
neurips-2023-near-optimal-learning-with-.tldr: Distribution-sensitive average Hölder smoothness yields sharper regression guarantees and nearly optimal algorithms, with matching realizable bounds up to logarithms.

paragraphs: Human–object interaction detection identifies actions linking people and objects in an image. Many Transformer-based detectors decode already assembled human–object pairs, restricting their ability to explore new combinations during decoding. LogicHOI changes this process so that the model can reason about people, actions, and objects together.

The method modifies Transformer self-attention to operate over human–action–object triplets and form novel interactions. Its reasoning is guided by affordances, meaning actions an object can support, and proxemics, meaning spatial relationships between humans and objects. These properties help constrain which proposed interactions are feasible.

The authors express those constraints in first-order logic and translate them into a continuous form that guides learning. Evaluations on V-COCO and HICO-DET show significant improvements over existing methods under both standard and zero-shot setups. The findings connect explicit interaction knowledge with improved detection and generalization: the model can use action possibilities and spatial relationships when considering combinations beyond those supplied as fixed pairs.
neurips-2023-neural-logic-human-object-i.tldr: LogicHOI combines Transformer attention with logical constraints on action possibilities and spatial relationships to improve interaction detection and zero-shot generalization.

paragraphs: Understanding an action requires relating words, visual content, and the order of events. The paper introduces ActionBench with Action Antonym and Video Reversal tasks to test multimodal alignment and temporal understanding. Tested video-language models perform near chance, suggesting that object recognition can serve as a shortcut on other action-related benchmarks.

Paxion addresses this gap by adding a Knowledge Patcher that learns action information and a Knowledge Fuser that integrates it with a frozen video-language model. The existing model remains fixed while the added components supply new capabilities. To train the patcher, the authors introduce Discriminative Video Dynamics Modeling, which links action text to the correct ordering of video frames.

The paper reports that Paxion and this training objective raise action-knowledge performance from approximately 50% to 80%. Performance on a broad set of object- and action-focused downstream tasks is maintained or improved. The results indicate that directly training temporal understanding can repair a specific weakness while retaining the usefulness of the original model’s learned capabilities.
neurips-2023-paxion-patching-action-know.tldr: Paxion adds action knowledge to frozen video-language models by training new components to connect action descriptions with frame order.

paragraphs: Language models trained on large web collections may encounter personally identifiable information. ProPILE is a probing tool intended to help the people associated with that information assess potential exposure through model-based services. Its focus is giving data subjects a way to investigate privacy intrusion involving their own information.

Users formulate prompts based on their own personally identifiable information and examine the model’s behavior. The paper demonstrates this approach with OPT-1.3B, trained on the publicly available Pile dataset. The demonstration considers hypothetical data subjects assessing the likelihood that their information included in that dataset could be revealed.

The tool is also intended for service providers, who can use more powerful prompts tuned to their own models to evaluate leakage. These two uses connect individual awareness with internal model assessment. The paper presents ProPILE as an initial step toward greater awareness and control over personal data on the web, with probing providing evidence about potential disclosure rather than itself removing the information from a model.
neurips-2023-propile-probing-privacy-lea.tldr: ProPILE helps people and model providers probe whether language models may reveal personally identifiable information.

paragraphs: Real-world image super-resolution must restore images affected by many different degradation processes. This paper views those processes as distinct learning tasks handled by one shared model. From that perspective, uneven restoration quality can arise because some tasks dominate training and interfere with learning the others.

The authors propose grouping tasks to address this competition. Their method identifies degradation tasks on which the super-resolution model performs poorly, organizes those tasks into several groups, and uses the groups to fine-tune the model. The approach targets weaknesses in the existing model while aiming to make knowledge transfer between tasks more effective.

Experiments show significantly improved performance across a wide range of degradation scenarios. The finding supports treating the organization of restoration tasks as an important part of training. A model’s challenge is not simply encountering numerous degradations; it must also learn them without allowing some to overwhelm others. The proposed grouping method provides a practical way to reduce that conflict through targeted fine-tuning.
neurips-2023-real-world-image-super-reso.tldr: Grouping poorly learned degradation tasks for fine-tuning reduces task competition and improves real-world image super-resolution.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single image supports real-world perception, but evaluation on carefully curated images can overlook disruptions encountered in practice. RoboDepth provides a dedicated test suite for examining how depth models respond to common corruptions. The motivation is especially relevant to systems operating in changing visual conditions.

The suite includes eighteen corruptions across three categories: weather and lighting, sensor failures and movement, and data-processing anomalies. The authors benchmark forty-two depth estimation models in indoor and outdoor scenes. This shared evaluation makes corruption resilience an explicit dimension of comparison rather than leaving it implicit in ordinary test performance.

The findings show that many leading depth models may be vulnerable to typical corruptions. The paper also examines design considerations involving pre-training, augmentation, input modality, model capacity, and learning paradigms. Its contribution is an evaluation platform and an empirical basis for studying robust depth estimation. The results motivate assessing performance under disrupted inputs alongside performance on curated data when judging a model’s practical reliability.
neurips-2023-robodepth-robust-out-of-dis.tldr: RoboDepth evaluates forty-two depth models under eighteen corruptions, revealing vulnerabilities that curated-data testing can overlook.

paragraphs: Estimating an object’s six-dimensional pose means determining its rotation and translation. This paper approaches that task by aligning a source point cloud with a model point cloud. It treats alignment as a denoising diffusion process that progressively refines a rigid transformation toward the desired pose.

During training, the forward process repeatedly perturbs the optimal transformation, and the reverse process learns to remove those perturbations step by step. Rotations and translations belong to SE(3), whose geometry differs from an ordinary linear space. The framework uses its associated linear Lie algebra to constrain transitions during both processes.

The authors derive a registration-specific variational lower bound as the learning objective. They also show that the denoising network can use a surrogate registration model, allowing the framework to accommodate different deep registration networks. Experiments report strong pose-estimation performance on TUD-L, LINEMOD, and Occluded-LINEMOD. The contribution connects iterative denoising with the geometry of rigid motion, providing a structured way to refine alignment in real-world pose-estimation tasks.
neurips-2023-se-3-diffusion-model-based-.tldr: An SE(3) diffusion framework estimates object pose by progressively denoising the rigid transformation aligning two point clouds.

paragraphs: Attractor networks represent information through persistent activity states supported by structured connections. Excitation–inhibition balanced networks instead use sparse, random connections to generate irregular firing. This paper asks how those two familiar descriptions of neural circuits can coexist despite their different structural demands.

The proposed circuit uses two sets of synapses with different strengths and timescales. Strong, fast connections support irregular firing, while weak, slow connections support continuous attractor dynamics. Simulations and theoretical analysis show that this arrangement can exhibit both kinds of behavior within the same network, consistent with the experimental picture described by the authors.

Compared with using only one set of synapses, the combined network reaches attractor states faster and preserves excitation–inhibition balance under localized input. The authors also apply it to a real-world tracking problem and demonstrate successful tracking of fast-moving objects. These findings offer a mechanism by which structured computation and irregular neural activity can work together, with their coexistence improving the studied network’s computational behavior.
neurips-2023-slow-and-weak-attractor-com.tldr: Separate fast, strong and slow, weak synapses allow a neural circuit to combine irregular balanced firing with useful attractor computation.

paragraphs: This paper studies what matrix spectra reveal about neural-network training when sample size grows proportionally with network width. Spectra summarize the distribution of values associated with a matrix’s main directions. The authors examine weight matrices and two kernel representations to connect changes in these distributions with feature learning.

For gradient descent with small constant learning rates, experiments show invariant weight spectra, supported by theoretical analysis. The paper also proves invariance of the bulk spectra of conjugate and neural tangent kernels, and observes similar behavior with small-rate stochastic gradient descent. Larger learning rates can produce an outlier whose eigenvector aligns with structure in the training data.

Adaptive gradient training produces heavy-tailed weight and kernel spectra alongside lower test error and feature learning. Simple examples explain circumstances where heavy tails can accompany better generalization. Related patterns appear in conventional networks trained on real-world data. The results distinguish stable bulk behavior, isolated spikes, and heavy tails as signatures associated with different training strategies, making spectral evolution informative about how learned representations change.
neurips-2023-spectral-evolution-and-inva.tldr: Different training strategies produce stable, spiked, or heavy-tailed matrix spectra that help characterize neural-network feature learning.

paragraphs: Video object segmentation follows an object through a video using an initial mask. Matching-based methods compare new frames with a memory of previously processed frames, but without adaptation they can struggle when test videos differ from training data. This paper examines adaptation under corruption, stylization, and transfer from simulated to real videos.

The authors explore both general test-time training strategies and strategies designed for video object segmentation. These include a mask cycle-consistency variant tailored to matching-based methods. The central idea is to update the model using the test video itself so that matching can work better under the conditions currently being encountered.

Experiments on common benchmarks show significant improvements. In the simulation-to-real setting, adaptation using a single test video recovers a substantial portion of the gain available from training on real videos. The paper also introduces DAVIS-C, which adds severe corruptions and stylizations to DAVIS. Improvements on this test set support the usefulness of test-time training even under the challenging shifts included in the evaluation.
neurips-2023-test-time-training-for-matc.tldr: Training on the test video improves matching-based object segmentation under corruptions, stylization, and simulation-to-real transfer.

paragraphs: Conversation often communicates more than the literal words state. An indirect answer can imply yes or no through context and everyday knowledge. This paper studies whether language models can resolve such implicatures, addressing an aspect of communication that ordinary performance evaluations may fail to capture.

The authors design a simple task requiring binary inferences and evaluate four categories of widely used language models. Even though the requested answer is only yes or no, models in three categories perform near chance. Models instruction-tuned at the level of individual examples perform significantly better on the task.

The contrast suggests that fine-tuning strategy matters for eliciting pragmatic understanding, rather than conversational use alone demonstrating that ability. The findings establish a concrete evaluation target: interpreting what a speaker conveys indirectly using context. The paper presents this study as a starting point for broader investigation of contextual language understanding and for developing more useful conversational models, with the evidence specifically grounded in the tested binary implicature task.
neurips-2023-the-goldilocks-of-pragmatic.tldr: A binary implicature task reveals near-chance performance in three model categories but substantially better results from example-level instruction tuning.

paragraphs: Exploring new hardware and software combinations can help advance machine learning, but efficient systems increasingly rely on specialized hardware and a narrow set of frameworks. This paper investigates the practical cost of moving beyond those familiar combinations. It asks how portable mainstream machine-learning frameworks actually are across hardware types.

The authors conduct a large-scale portability study examining both available functionality and performance. They find that frameworks can lose more than 40% of their key functions when moved to different hardware. Even functions that remain available can suffer extreme slowdowns, so successful execution alone does not establish practical portability.

These findings identify an exploration cost associated with specialization. Researchers considering alternative systems may face missing capabilities, poor performance, or both, making experimentation harder. The paper argues that this friction can impede innovation as software and hardware evolve together around established stacks. Its contribution is to quantify portability problems and connect them to the freedom to explore different computing systems in machine-learning research.
neurips-2023-the-grand-illusion-the-myth.tldr: A portability study finds major functionality losses and slowdowns across hardware, revealing an exploration cost of specialized ML systems.

paragraphs: Robots often adapt previously learned motion policies when tasks or operating conditions change. This paper focuses on policies represented by Gaussian mixture models, which combine several Gaussian distributions. It argues that policy optimization can benefit from explicitly respecting this probabilistic structure when modifying a robot’s behavior.

The authors formulate policy optimization as an optimal transport problem and describe updates through a Wasserstein gradient flow over Gaussian mixtures. The Wasserstein distance constrains how far a policy moves between updates, supporting a more stable optimization process. They also use Bures–Wasserstein geometry to optimize the individual Gaussian components with Riemannian methods.

Evaluations cover reaching, collision avoidance, and tasks with multiple goals. The method outperforms common policy-optimization baselines in task success and in producing low-variance solutions. The contribution is a geometry-aware way to adapt structured motion policies: both the overall mixture update and its Gaussian components are optimized using distances and geometry suited to probability distributions, with the reported benefits demonstrated in the evaluated robotic settings.
neurips-2023-wasserstein-gradient-flows-.tldr: Optimal-transport geometry guides Gaussian-mixture robot policy updates, improving task success and reducing solution variance in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Some robust image classifiers have input gradients that align with human perception, giving them rudimentary image generation and restoration abilities despite classification training. This paper explains that phenomenon through off-manifold robustness. The relevant condition is greater robustness to changes away from the data manifold than to changes along it.

The authors theoretically show that this condition makes input gradients lie approximately on the data manifold, explaining their perceptual alignment. They also show that Bayes-optimal models satisfy the condition. Empirical studies find it in robust models trained using gradient-norm regularization, randomized smoothing, and projected-gradient-descent adversarial training.

To measure alignment, the paper compares classifier gradients with gradients from generative models and finds a strong correlation with off-manifold robustness. It distinguishes weak, Bayes-aligned, and excessive robustness regimes according to on- and off-manifold behavior. These regimes affect both accuracy and gradient alignment. The findings therefore explain why the direction of robustness matters, rather than treating robustness as a single quantity whose increase always has the same effect.
neurips-2023-which-models-have-perceptua.tldr: Greater robustness away from the data manifold explains why some classifiers have gradients aligned with human perception.
